A sea star has a simple eyespot at the tip of each arm.
Some sea stars can regrow a whole arm if they lose one.

centipod.where: Soil, leaf litter and under logs and rocks almost everywhere on land
centipod.size: The largest kinds grow to about 30 cm (12 inches) long

facts.text: The name centipede means 'hundred feet,' but no centipede has exactly 100 legs.
Centipedes always have an odd number of pairs of legs, from 15 pairs to 191 pairs.
A centipede's first pair of legs became venom claws for catching food.

stepant.where: The Sahara Desert of North Africa

facts.text: When scientists gave a related Saharan desert ant tiny stilts, it walked past its nest, which showed it keeps track of its steps.
Silver ants are covered in shiny hairs that reflect sunlight and help them shed heat.
They come out of the nest for only about ten minutes a day, in heat of around 47 °C (117 °F).

webangle.where: Gardens, fields and forests around the world

facts.text: An orb web has straight spokes going out from the middle and a sticky spiral laid on top.
The spider builds the spokes first from non-sticky silk and adds the sticky spiral last.
Many orb-weavers eat their old web and spin a brand-new one each day.

spiralnaut.where: Deep waters near coral reefs of the western Pacific Ocean, such as off Australia and Japan

facts.text: As it grows, a chambered nautilus builds new, bigger chambers in its spiral shell and moves into them.
Many people say the nautilus shell follows the golden ratio, but measurements show it does not.
A nautilus has about 90 tentacles, and none of them have suckers.

numbanzee.where: Forests and savannas of equatorial Africa

facts.text: A chimpanzee named Ayumu at Kyoto University remembered the order of numbers on a touch screen better than university students.
Some scientists point out that Ayumu had practiced the game much more than the students had.
Some wild chimpanzees in West Africa crack open hard nuts with stones.

lexibo.where: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River

facts.text: A bonobo named Kanzi learned to talk using a keyboard with over 300 picture symbols called lexigrams.
Researchers were teaching Kanzi's mother, but Kanzi picked up the symbols on his own.
Bonobos share food with others, even strangers.

wordcollie.where: First bred near the border of England and Scotland, now found worldwide

facts.text: A border collie named Chaser learned the names of 1,022 toys.
Chaser could figure out a new toy's name by ruling out all the names she already knew.
Border collies were bred to herd sheep, and they use a hard stare called 'the eye' to move the flock.

chirpuga.size: Males can grow up to 5.5 meters (18 feet) long

facts.text: Belugas are nicknamed 'sea canaries' because of their high-pitched calls.
The round bump on a beluga's head, called the melon, changes shape as it makes sounds.
Baby belugas are born gray and slowly turn white as they grow up.

mynatter.where: Forests of South and Southeast Asia, from India to southern China and the Philippines

facts.text: Hill mynas kept by people are famous for copying sounds, especially the human voice.
Many people think wild hill mynas copy other birds, but they do not.
Hill mynas have bright yellow patches of skin, called wattles, on their heads.

qiloom.where: China, with similar stories in Japan and Korea
qiloom.story: In Chinese legend, the qilin is a rare and gentle creature with hooves and shimmering scales. When a qilin appears, it is said to be a sign that a wise and good leader or teacher is coming.

facts.text: In the stories, a qilin's feet never harm any living thing, not even grass.
One legend says a qilin appeared to the mother of the great teacher Confucius just before he was born.
In the 1400s, a giraffe brought to China after Zheng He's voyages was thought to be a qilin, and today 'kirin' is the Japanese word for giraffe.

rocquill.where: Arabic and Persian tales of the Middle East
rocquill.story: The roc is a giant bird from Middle Eastern tales, so big it was said to carry off elephants. It appears in the stories of Sinbad the Sailor in One Thousand and One Nights.

facts.text: On his second voyage, Sinbad finds a roc egg so big it looks like a huge white dome, 50 paces around.
The traveler Marco Polo also wrote about the roc, and people later linked it to the island of Madagascar.
Some think the giant eggs of Madagascar's elephant bird, which could not fly, helped inspire the legend.

gargrim.where: Old churches and buildings of Europe, especially France
gargrim.story: Gargoyles are carved stone creatures that perch on old European churches. People said they guarded the building against evil, and a French legend tells of a dragon named La Gargouille near the city of Rouen.

facts.text: Many gargoyles are rain spouts that carry water off the roof so it does not wear away the walls.
The word gargoyle comes from the French word gargouille, which is linked to the throat and to a gurgling sound.
Carved creatures that do not spout water are more properly called grotesques.

sirenade.story: In Greek myths, the sirens were magical singers who lived on a rocky island. Their songs were so beautiful that sailors would steer toward them and forget about going home.

facts.text: In early Greek art, sirens were shown as large birds with human faces.
In the Odyssey, the hero Odysseus has his sailors plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast so he can hear the song safely.
In another story, the musician Orpheus played his music more beautifully than the sirens, so the sailors could not hear them.

talosteel.where: Ancient Greece, on the island of Crete
talosteel.story: In Greek myth, Talos was a huge man made of bronze who guarded the island of Crete. He ran around the whole island three times every day and threw boulders at ships that came too close.

facts.text: One version of the myth says the god Zeus gave Talos to Europa, the mother of King Minos, to protect the island.
Talos had a single vein running from his neck to his ankle, closed with a bronze nail.
Ancient coins from Phaistos, a city on Crete, show Talos with wings, throwing a stone.

glowplume.where: Slavic folk tales of Russia and Eastern Europe
glowplume.story: In Slavic folk tales, the firebird is a glowing bird from a faraway land that comes at night to eat golden apples in the tsar's garden. Brave heroes go on long quests to find it.

facts.text: In the stories, one firebird feather keeps glowing and can light up a large room.
A firebird quest usually begins when someone finds one of its lost tail feathers.
The composer Igor Stravinsky wrote a famous ballet called The Firebird, first performed in Paris in 1910.

bakumist.where: Japan, based on older stories from China
bakumist.story: In Japanese folklore, the baku is a gentle spirit that eats bad dreams. A child who wakes from a nightmare can say 'Baku-san, come eat my dream' three times.

facts.text: A book from the early 1600s describes the baku with an elephant's trunk, a cow's tail and a tiger's paws.
The Japanese baku comes from an older Chinese creature called the mo.
Today, baku is also the Japanese word for the tapir, a real animal with a short trunk.

yetitan.where: Himalayan folklore of Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan
yetitan.story: In Himalayan folklore, the yeti is a big, hairy creature said to roam the high snowy mountains. It is a legend, and there is no proof that yetis are real.

facts.text: The nickname 'Abominable Snowman' came from a mistranslation in a 1921 newspaper story.
In 1951, explorer Eric Shipton photographed large footprints in the snow, but many think melting snow made ordinary tracks look bigger.
When scientists tested the DNA of hair and bones said to come from yetis, they turned out to be from bears and even a dog.

mantido.where: Native to China, Japan, Korea and the far east of Russia. People later brought it to North America too.
mantido.size: Up to about 11 cm (4 inches) long

facts.text: A kung fu style called Northern Praying Mantis is named after this kind of insect. Stories say it began in Shandong, China, when a fighter watched a brave mantis.
Chinese mantises can be green or brown, which helps them hide among plants.
A mother mantis makes a foamy egg case that can hold up to 300 eggs.

cranekick.where: Wetlands of China, Japan, Korea and the far east of Russia
cranekick.size: About 1.5 m (5 feet) tall, with wings more than 2 m (7 feet) across

facts.text: White Crane kung fu comes from Fujian, China. The legend says a young woman named Fang Qiniang learned it by watching a crane move. The story does not say which kind of crane it was.
The red on its head is bare skin, not feathers. It gets brighter in mating season.
Crane pairs call and dance together. This helps them stay a team and tells other cranes the area is taken.

monkido.where: Mountain forests in four provinces of central China: Sichuan, Gansu, Shaanxi and Hubei
monkido.size: Males are about 58 to 68 cm (2 feet) long, not counting the tail. Females are smaller.

facts.text: Monkey style kung fu copies the way monkeys move. Fighters squat, roll, tumble and even make monkey faces.
Its home gets lots of snow. Scientists think it can handle the cold better than any other monkey or ape, not counting people.
Its main food is lichen that grows on trees. It also eats leaves, buds, fruits, seeds and bark.

tigrifu.where: Once lived across the forests and hills of southern China. Today it lives only in zoos and breeding parks.
tigrifu.size: A big male can be about 2.3 to 2.6 m (8 feet) long

facts.text: Tiger is one of the five animal styles of Southern Chinese kung fu. The others are crane, leopard, snake and dragon.
No one has found a wild South China tiger since the 1980s. It may be gone from the wild. But in 2019, about 150 lived in care in China, and people are working to help them.

paddlet.where: Rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania
paddlet.size: About as long as a house cat

facts.text: The platypus is one of only a few mammals that lay eggs.

coatikit.where: Forests of the southwestern United States, Mexico and Central America
coatikit.size: About as long as a house cat, with a tail just as long

voltewe.where: First bred in Spain and Portugal, and now raised around the world, especially in Australia and New Zealand
voltewe.size: A Merino fleece usually weighs about 4 kg

possumoon.where: Most of the United States, Mexico and Central America
possumoon.size: About the size of a house cat

lunaflit.size: Wings up to about 11 cm (4.5 inches) across

aardshade.where: Dry grasslands and scrub of eastern and southern Africa

galagleam.where: Forests and woodlands across Africa south of the Sahara
galagleam.size: About the size of a squirrel

honkabat.where: Forests and rivers of west and central Africa
honkabat.size: Wings nearly 1 m (3 feet) across, the biggest bat in mainland Africa

solenox.where: The Caribbean islands of Cuba and Hispaniola
solenox.size: About 30 cm (1 foot) long, plus a long tail

lorishade.where: Forests of South and Southeast Asia
lorishade.size: About 25 to 38 cm (10 to 15 inches) long

hootmonk.where: Forests of Central and South America
hootmonk.size: About 30 cm (1 foot) long, plus its tail

glidewisp.where: Forests of Australia and New Guinea
glidewisp.size: About 16 to 21 cm (6 to 8 inches) long, plus its tail

solarion.story: In Greek myth, Leo is the Nemean lion that the hero Heracles defeated. Its stars were placed in the sky as a lion.

delphinova.story: In Greek myth, a dolphin helped the sea god Poseidon, and was placed among the stars as a thank-you.

ursastar.basedOn: Ursa Major, the Great Bear constellation

facts.text: The seven brightest stars of Ursa Major make the shape called the Big Dipper.

dracostar.story: In Greek myth, Draco is the dragon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides.

cosmobill.where: Rivers and lakes of eastern Australia, and in this game, the stars

cobrafu.where: Forests of India and Southeast Asia

pardojo.where: Forests and grasslands of India and nearby countries

talonfu.where: Grasslands (steppes) from eastern Europe across Central Asia to Mongolia

roadzoom.where: Deserts and dry scrub of the southwestern United States and Mexico

snapjaw.where: Rivers, lakes and swamps of the southeastern United States
snapjaw.size: Up to about 80 cm (31 inches) shell length

springbolt.where: Dry grasslands and deserts of southern Africa

braypen.where: Coasts and islands of South Africa and Namibia

storkwing.where: Europe in summer, Africa in winter

carpabear.where: Forests of the Carpathian Mountains in Romania and nearby countries
carpabear.size: Adults stand about 1 m (3 feet) tall at the shoulder on all fours

tuskhog.where: Rainforests of West and Central Africa

leafviper.where: Rainforests of West and Central Africa
leafviper.size: Usually about 1.2 to 1.5 m (4 to 5 feet) long

mandrilux.where: Rainforests of Central Africa, including Gabon, Cameroon and the Republic of the Congo
mandrilux.size: About 55 to 95 cm (2 to 3 feet) long, the largest monkey

congopeak.where: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo

leoseal.size: About 2.4 to 3.5 m (8 to 11 feet) long

snowflit.where: Antarctica and the icy Southern Ocean

loonsong.where: Northern lakes of Canada and the northern United States, and coasts in winter

hornsquirt.where: Dry plains and deserts of the south-central United States and northern Mexico

rackit.where: Forests, wetlands and towns across most of North America

crestalon.where: Near lakes, rivers and coasts across North America

leapcroc.size: Usually about 2 to 2.5 m (6.5 to 8 feet) long

digdillo.where: Forests and grasslands of South America

macawsong.where: Woodlands and wetlands of central South America, including Brazil's Pantanal

dartblaze.where: Rainforests of Central and South America

trunkseal.where: Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands and seas

barraclad.where: Warm oceans around the world, including the Caribbean
barraclad.size: Commonly up to about 1.5 m (5 feet) long

toothfrost.where: Cold waters of the Southern Ocean around Antarctica

gobblaze.where: Forests and fields across much of North America

bluepinch.where: Coasts and bays of the western Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico

squirrust.where: Forests across Europe and northern Asia

leapsalmon.where: Rivers and the North Atlantic Ocean

sturgeonplate.where: The Caspian and Black Seas and rivers like the Danube and Volga

bustarboom.where: Open grasslands and farmland of Europe and Asia, with many in Hungary and Spain

molediggs.where: Fields and woods across much of Europe

sealmonk.where: Coasts and sea caves of the eastern Mediterranean and northwest Africa

coilball.where: Grasslands and open forests of West and Central Africa

goldcatshade.where: Rainforests of Central and West Africa

goliathorn.where: Rainforests of Central and West Africa

honeyfu.where: Africa, the Middle East and India

paintpup.where: Savannas and woodlands of southern and eastern Africa

sandshade.where: Deserts of North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia

gharialance.where: Rivers of northern India and Nepal

slothroar.where: Forests and grasslands of India, Sri Lanka and Nepal

manulmist.where: Cold grasslands and mountains of Central Asia, including Mongolia and Tibet

otterkit.where: Coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean, including California and Alaska
otterkit.size: About 1 to 1.5 m (3.3 to 5 feet) long

quokkit.where: Rottnest Island and southwestern Western Australia

fenneckit.where: Sahara Desert and other deserts of North Africa

jawstorm.where: Cool coastal oceans worldwide, including South Africa

thylashade.where: Tasmania, and long ago mainland Australia and New Guinea

dodobell.where: The island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean
